passage: Okay, so this is embarrassing, but Chetan and I have a streak going, forty days of daily snaps, and I started reading way too much into it. Last week he sent me a heart, and I spent the whole evening thinking, does that mean something? Then he sent the same heart to our whole cricket group and I felt silly. My cousin said, "Just ask him." So I texted, "Are we just friends? 🙂" and he said, "Yeah bro, we're best friends, hearts are just how I say good night." And honestly, I felt relieved. Some people use a heart the way other people say okay. Now I ask instead of decoding, and I sleep better. Saurabh, signing off.

qa.q: How long had Saurabh and Chetan kept their snap streak?
qa.a: They had kept a streak of forty days of daily snaps.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel silly when Chetan sent the heart to the whole group?
qa.a: Saurabh realised the heart, which Chetan sends to everyone, had been over-read. Saurabh also felt a little embarrassed about the whole evening spent wondering.

qa.q: What would you advise Saurabh to do when a message seems unclear again?
qa.a: Ask the person directly, in a friendly way, instead of guessing from a heart or a streak.

qa.q: How might Chetan see the heart he sends?
qa.a: As a casual way of saying good night to friends, not as a sign of something more. 🙂

grounding: Digital fondness such as hearts and streaks is ambiguous, and asking directly is wiser than over-reading.

passage: I sit behind Bidisha in maths, so I saw a lot. Last Friday she checked her phone under the desk eight or nine times, her thumb hovering. Later she told me, sort of laughing, that her streak with a friend was going to break and the friend hadn't even liked her new post. She said it lightly, but she kept turning her phone face down and up again. I couldn't tell if she was hurt or just annoyed. At lunch she typed something and sent it before she could change her mind. Ten minutes later she showed me the reply: 'Sorry, my phone screen cracked!' She let out a long breath and put the phone away. Nazia.

qa.q: Where did Nazia sit in maths?
qa.a: Nazia sat behind Bidisha in maths.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have been feeling when she kept checking her phone?
qa.a: She might have been worried or hurt that her friend had not liked the post and that the streak might break. Nazia admits not being sure, since Bidisha said it lightly.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do that helped?
qa.a: She sent a message to check instead of assuming the friend was upset with her, and got a simple explanation.

qa.q: How might the friend with the cracked screen have seen the silence?
qa.a: The friend may not have noticed how much a missing like could mean, since the friend's phone screen was cracked.

grounding: A missing like and a streak cause worry, and asking directly clears the ambiguity, seen by an observer.

passage:
Monday: Irfan noticed Ojas had liked six of his old photos in one evening, all from last summer. Irfan stared at the screen for a long time and felt his heart speed up.
Wednesday: Ojas sent a 🤍 on Irfan's cricket story, then a meme with "us" typed under it. Irfan typed three replies and deleted them all. His friend said a white heart meant something serious. Another friend said it meant nothing.
Saturday: At the nets, Irfan finally asked. "The hearts and all the likes... do they mean anything? I don't want to guess."
Ojas laughed, not unkindly. "Oh! Our team group sends white hearts to everyone. It just means 'good one.' And I was scrolling back to find the batting video for Coach."
Irfan felt his face go hot, then relief. "Okay. Good to know."
"You're my best batting partner, though," Ojas added. "That part I mean."

qa.q: How many of Irfan's old photos did Ojas like in one evening?
qa.a: Ojas had liked six of his old photos in one evening.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling on Wednesday when he typed and deleted three replies?
qa.a: He was nervous and unsure, hopeful the heart meant something more but afraid of misreading it.

qa.q: What small step helped Irfan stop guessing?
qa.a: Asking Ojas directly at the nets, because emojis and likes meant different things in different groups.

qa.q: How does Ojas see the white heart compared with Irfan's friend?
qa.a: For Ojas it is an everyday "good one" used in the team group, while Irfan's friend read it as something serious.

grounding: The three beats show digital signs of fondness being ambiguous and a teenager asking directly instead of reading too much into them.

passage:
Ira, you think your generation invented confusing signals? Sit, let your Jyoti Masi tell you about missed calls.
When I was fifteen, a boy from my tuition gave my house one missed call every night at nine. One ring, then nothing. My friend Sulekha said, "One ring means I love you, everyone knows." My cousin said, "It means he's too cheap to pay for a call."
For a month I lay awake inventing stories. I even wrote his initials in my rough book.
Then I asked him outside tuition, shaking like a leaf: "Why do you ring every night?"
He looked puzzled. "Your mother asked my mother to check you reached home. My mother made me do it."
I was so embarrassed I missed my bus. But honestly, it was a relief. I stopped reading love letters into one ring after that.

qa.q: At what time did the boy give Jyoti's house a missed call?
qa.a: He gave one missed call every night at nine.

qa.q: How was Jyoti feeling when she asked the boy outside tuition?
qa.a: She was very nervous, shaking like a leaf, because she had been hoping the call meant love and was afraid of the answer.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jyoti's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Asking the boy directly ended a month of guessing, because only he could say what the one ring meant.

qa.q: How might the boy have seen the nightly missed calls?
qa.a: To him it was just a chore his mother made him do, so he was puzzled that it could mean anything more.

grounding: The elder's story shows a signal of apparent fondness being ambiguous and asking directly clearing it up.

passage:
Gautam's family trip to the hills had one problem: the guest house had no network except on one rock behind the kitchen. On day two his streak with Ganga broke at 47 days.
Ganga noticed at breakfast in Delhi. Then she saw his only message, sent from the rock at dawn: "all good here 🙂".
In her group, a plain 🙂 meant "I'm annoyed but whatever." She read it five times. Had she done something? Was he bored of her?
She almost sent a cold reply. Instead, she waited.
When Gautam got back on Sunday, she met him at the colony gate. "Can I ask what the 🙂 meant? And the streak?"
He looked baffled. "The smile meant smile! And I had one bar on a rock, Ganga. I climbed it at six just to message you."
She laughed, embarrassed and oddly touched.

qa.q: At how many days did the streak break?
qa.a: The streak broke at 47 days.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she read Gautam's message five times?
qa.a: She felt anxious and hurt, worried the plain smile meant he was annoyed or bored of her.

qa.q: Which choice of Ganga's worked, and why?
qa.a: Waiting and then asking directly worked, because the smile meant something different to Gautam and the broken streak was about network, not feelings.

qa.q: What was it like for Gautam to find out how his message was read?
qa.a: He was baffled, since for him a smile meant a smile and he had climbed a rock at dawn just to send it.

grounding: The scene shows a digital sign of affection and a broken streak being read wrongly across groups, and asking directly clearing it up.

passage: Ganga-didi had moved to Bengaluru for her first job in June, and since then she had sent Manoj a meme every single night: cats in hostels, engineers crying, a mango in sunglasses. Manoj, in the family's Indore flat, replied to every one with a single thumbs-up 👍. Nothing else. After two months Ganga called Maa. "Is he angry with me? Just thumbs, like I'm his tuition teacher." Maa laughed and passed the phone over. "Manoj, your didi thinks you hate her memes." Manoj went red. "I don't hate them. The thumbs means got it, I saw, still here. Everyone in my class does that." Then, quieter: "I screenshot all of them. I have a folder called Didi." There was a pause on the line. "You could have just said," Ganga said, her voice wobbly. That night he typed: "👍 and also I miss you."

qa.q: Where did Ganga move for her first job?
qa.a: Ganga moved to Bengaluru for her first job in June.

qa.q: What does Manoj's folder called Didi suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Manoj felt real affection and missed Ganga; the bare thumbs-up was his class's way of saying 'I saw', not coldness, even though it read as distant.

qa.q: What could Ganga have done sooner?
qa.a: Ganga could have asked Manoj directly what the thumbs-up meant instead of worrying for two months and checking through Maa.

qa.q: How did the thumbs-up look from Ganga's side?
qa.a: To Ganga it looked flat, like a reply to a tuition teacher, so she worried Manoj was angry with her.

grounding: It shows a teenager's affection hidden inside a bare digital reaction whose meaning differs between groups, and a direct question clearing it up.
